name: Deploy into siege mode
summary: The unit stops and plants itself: stabilisers or legs dig in, a soldier builds a small nest, a hovering flier sets down or locks onto one spot. While planted it cannot move, and in return it gets a stronger stationary mode: a heavier or longer-reaching weapon it can't fire on the move, more armour and a full turret arc, a faster-firing locked stance, or a field or building that works only while it stays put. Setting up takes a moment and packing up often does too, so planting is a commitment to a spot. The design levers are what the mode gives, how long set-up and pack-up take, whether the mobile weapon still works, the arc and any dead zone close in, and what can force it out of the mode.
counterplay: Catch it on the move, or while it sets up or packs up, when neither its mobile weapon nor its planted one is fully working.
Flank or dive it: it can't step away, and many planted weapons have a narrow arc or a blind zone right next to the unit.
Come from the air: most planted modes only hit the ground, and the siege units of Red Alert 2 and Tiberian Sun fall to air attack.
Out-range it with artillery or bombard its spot: a unit that can't move can't dodge.
Take away its spotters: long planted weapons often reach past their own sight and need teammates to see targets for them.
Force it out with a hook or pull, a knockdown, a sleep, a pin or a hack (Overwatch threw its sentry Bastion out of the mode with these), or pin or infest a mobile one so it can't deploy at all.
Walk around its field or arc instead of through it, and make it pack up to follow you.

other_examples.note: Siege mode gives up all movement for a heavier cannon with splash that reaches well past what the tank itself can see, so it needs other units to spot. It can't hit enemies right next to it, and its splash can hurt friendly units near targets that close in. Players split tanks into groups so a column doesn't plant all at once in the wrong spot, and screen them with other units. It is weak against air and against fast melee units that reach the blind zone. From Legacy of the Void's beta until patch 3.8, a medivac could pick up a planted tank and drop it ready to fire after a short delay.

A gunship that anchors in the air over a ground circle it picks a short way off. Anchored, it can't move and fires only at ground units inside that circle, very hard, and it sees that spot. To move the circle it must go back to its anti-air fighter mode and anchor again; each change takes about a second. Ground units walk out of the circle, and it can't attack buildings.

Nod's light tank burrows its front into the ground: it can't move, but it gains much better protection and a full turret arc, so Nod can put a turret almost anywhere; it has to dig out before driving off. Dug in, it holds up well against GDI's sonic tank (the Disruptor) and its railgun super-walker (the Mammoth Mk. II), while in a straight fight in the open it loses to the Titan walker.

sources.title: Tick tank, Command & Conquer Wiki

sources.title: Mammoth Mk. II, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Describes the Mammoth Mk. II as a four-legged super-heavy walker with railguns.

sources.title: Juggernaut (Firestorm), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Calls the Titan a walker that outclasses the Tick.

other_examples.note: Both artillery units fire only once they have planted stabilisers, and can't move while planted. The Juggernaut walker takes a couple of seconds to plant, and to hit anything outside its reach it must rise, walk and plant again. Both are fragile and fall to air attack, and computer-controlled ones stay planted unless a target slips inside their minimum range.

sources.title: Artillery (Tiberian Sun), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Its quote box copies the Tiberian Sun manual's entry.

other_examples.note: It has to lower four stabilisers before it can fire, which takes a few seconds each way, and it sometimes packs and unpacks again between targets that are already in reach. It is slow, thinly armoured and has a minimum range, but its shells wreck infantry, tanks and buildings alike from far away, and nothing can shoot them down.

The basic Allied rifleman can plant himself behind a ring of sandbags with a heavier machine gun that reaches further and hits harder, at the price of not moving at all; massed planted GIs hold off most ground attacks. Yuri's Revenge's Guardian GI plants a steel barricade instead, which also stops vehicles from crushing him, and swaps his rifle for long-range anti-tank missiles that hit vehicles and aircraft but do little to infantry.

sources.title: GI, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Its official description box copies the Red Alert 2 manual's entry.

other_examples.note: A hover vehicle with twin miniguns that anchors itself to fire a long-range artillery cannon. Anchored, it can neither move nor use the miniguns and needs scouting to use its reach, and the markers where its shells will land are shown to every player, so it mostly hits buildings and slow units. It can't anchor on water.

sources.title: Special ability (Red Alert 3), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Lists every unit's ability with the in-game button text; Red Alert 3 files it as a toggle mode.

other_examples.note: After a field upgrade, British tanks can go hull down: sandbags rise around the tank over several seconds while it keeps firing. Once dug in it can't move, but it takes less damage and fewer shots get through its armour. The dig-in can't be cancelled halfway, while leaving it is instant.

sources.title: Cromwell Tank, Company of Heroes Wiki

other_examples.note: A light, fast wheeled tank hunter that can lock down, lowering itself and pulling in its rear wheels, to fire a larger explosive railgun shell as artillery; a bought armour upgrade adds protection for the locked-down state.

shooter_analogues.note: The heavy suit can lock itself in place: it can't move and can only aim across its front half, but its weapons fire, reload and send shots faster, and blasts can't knock it around. Locking takes about two seconds, during which it already has the limits but not yet the bonus; unlocking is instant.

The tank has to be stopped to anchor; anchored, its main cannon's shells fly half again faster but it can't move, while the gunner's weapon is unchanged. Anchoring takes a second and leaving it is instant.

shooter_analogues.unit: Bastion (Configuration: Sentry, later Assault and Artillery)
shooter_analogues.note: In the original Overwatch, Bastion could turn into a sentry: a stationary gatling turret that took less damage, and being hacked, put to sleep, pinned, hooked or knocked down threw it back out of the mode. Overwatch 2's rework turned that form into a slow-moving, time-limited assault mode, while its ultimate still roots it in place to call down up to three artillery shells.

sources.title: Bastion, Overwatch Wiki
sources.version: Overwatch 2 as of October 2026, with the page's history of Overwatch 1 abilities

player_translation.summary: One key plants the unit: after a short, visible set-up it becomes a stationary emplacement with a stronger weapon, more armour or a field, and the same key packs it up again after a short delay. The player trades mobility for holding a spot, and the team decides which spot is worth holding.
as_user: You pick the spot before the fight reaches it: a choke point, a ridge with long sight lines, the flank your team must hold. Planting where the enemy will come is the skill.
Set-up is your danger window: for about a second neither weapon is fully ready. Pack-up is quicker but not instant, so you plan your exit before you need it.

Planted, you get a clear payoff: longer reach aimed at the cursor (often past your own sight, so a teammate's spotting matters), a heavier gun, less damage taken and a full turret arc, or a field around you.
You can't dodge, so you rely on cover, the planted armour and teammates to stop divers; a blind zone right next to you is common.
as_target: A planted enemy is a fixed, telegraphed threat: its reach and arc are drawn on the ground, so you go around it, come at it from its blind side or from the air.
Its set-up and pack-up animations are your openings: dive it then, or flank it when it has planted in the wrong place.
A pull, knockdown or stun throws it out of the mode and into a fresh set-up, which is the moment your team kills it.
Artillery and lobbed weapons hit it easily because it can't move.
teammates: Scouts and spotters mark targets past its sight so its long weapon can fire.
Shield, cover-building and repair classes keep the planted unit alive, and escorts guard its blind zone.
A transport can carry it to a spot and set it down ready (the carried variant).
On the enemy side, divers and fliers coordinate to break a planted line, and a pull or stun sets it up for the team.
controls: WASD moves and the mouse aims as usual. Q starts planting where the unit stands (a moving unit brakes to a stop first); Q again packs up.

Planted: left mouse fires the planted weapon at the cursor within its arc and reach, and the mouse turns the turret within the arc. The mobile weapon is silent unless the variant keeps it. WASD does nothing while planted.
The pattern spends one counted key (Q). The universal keys work as on every unit; bailing out of a planted vehicle leaves the hull where it stands.
Zone-anchor variant: holding Q shows the circle at the cursor, releasing confirms it. Land-to-deploy variant: the same Q lands and lifts off.
feedback: A clear set-up animation with a progress ring and a heavy thud when planted, and a different sound on pack-up.
Planted: stabilisers, sandbags or a lowered hull visible from above, and the weapon's reach and arc drawn faintly on the ground for everyone, with any blind zone shaded.
HUD: mode icon, set-up and pack-up progress, and a warning when an enemy enters the blind zone or moves behind the arc.
Minimap: planted units show to their own team as fixed emplacements with their reach.
changes_from_rts: RTS siege units lean on other units for spotting and protection; here one player is one unit, so the planted mode must leave the player things to do (aim, turn the arc, pick targets) and a way out.
Set-up and pack-up must be short (about a second, not the several seconds of the Nuke Cannon or a hull-down tank) but clearly visible, or the unit is either a death trap or a free turret.
Weapons that reach past the unit's sight need team spotting (pings, marks); without it, give them a reach the camera can show.
Hard disables (pull, knockdown, stun) should knock it out of the mode, so a planted player is never a permanent fixture.

A fully static player form is hard to make fun to play and to fight: Overwatch replaced its immobile sentry Bastion with a slow, timed form. Planted time should be a choice the player makes, not the whole job.
A flier that lands (the Siege Chopper) becomes a ground target; a top-down camera must show that change plainly (shadow gone, landing ring).
A field that only works while planted (the Desolator) is the planted-field variant of leave-hazard-zone; this pattern covers the planting.

team_play.notes: A planted unit holds ground for the team but needs escorts for its blind zone and spotters for its reach; the enemy team must bring divers, fliers or artillery to break it, and a planted line can be the trap the team pulls enemies into.

notes: A small state machine (mobile, setting up, planted, packing up) plus a weapon swap and a movement lock; a stationary unit is easy to network.
Arcs, reach rings and blind zones need drawing on the ground in the top-down view.
Variants cost more: a landing flier changes target layer, a building form needs structure rules, a carried unit needs transport hooks.
Edge cases: set-up interrupted by a stun, planting on slopes, water or inside cover, and forced pack-up when knocked out of the mode.
A planted unit with long reach and armour can lock a choke point for a whole round; the RTS answer is air and artillery, which the roster must also offer.
Too slow a set-up makes it useless; too fast makes it a mobile unit with free bonuses and invites plant-and-cancel tricks.
Several planted units with overlapping reach or stacking fields (Red Alert 2 Desolator fields add up) can make an area impassable.
Reach past sight with free shared vision turns it into artillery that can't be answered.
The planted state is easy to read from above if the silhouette changes clearly (stabilisers, sandbags, lowered hull).
Its reach and blind zone must be shown, or deaths to shells from beyond the screen feel random.
A landed flier becoming a ground target must be obvious to both teams.

variants.name: Siege gun
variants.summary: Planted, the same job gets a heavier, longer-reaching weapon it can't fire on the move, often with splash and a blind zone close in.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II Siege Tank, Tiberian Sun Artillery and Juggernaut, Generals Nuke Cannon, Red Alert 2 GI

variants.name: Weapon swap
variants.summary: Planted, it swaps its weapon for one with a different job: a rifle becomes anti-tank missiles, a machine gun becomes a howitzer, miniguns become an artillery cannon.
variants.seen_in: Yuri's Revenge Guardian GI and Siege Chopper, Uprising Pacifier FAV

variants.name: Dig in
variants.summary: Planting adds armour and a full turret arc instead of a new gun, turning the unit into a turret it can place anywhere.
variants.seen_in: Tiberian Sun Tick Tank, Company of Heroes hull-down British tanks

adds_strengths.why: Dug in, it takes much less damage and turns its gun all the way round: a turret it can place anywhere.

counters.why: Slow ground units have to walk into its prepared field of fire and can't get out of it quickly.

variants.name: Lockdown
variants.summary: Planted, its own weapons fire, reload and send shots faster and blasts can't push it, but it aims only across its front.

adds_strengths.why: Locked down, its weapons fire, reload and send shots faster, and blasts can't push it around.

adds_weaknesses.why: Locked down, it can't move and aims only across its front, so flankers get behind it.

counters.why: Slow ground units have to walk into its prepared field of fire and can't get out of it quickly.

variants.name: Marked shells
variants.summary: A planted artillery weapon whose landing spots are marked for every player before the slow shells arrive, so it punishes only targets that stand still.

adds_weaknesses.why: Its shells are slow and their landing spots are marked for everyone, so only slow or still targets get hit.

variants.name: Land to deploy
variants.summary: A hovering flier sets down to bring out its planted weapon; on the ground it becomes a ground target until it lifts off again.

adds_weaknesses.why: Landed, it is a ground target that ordinary ground weapons reach, and lifting off again takes a moment.

variants.name: Zone anchor
variants.summary: It picks a circle a short way off and anchors over it: it can't move and fires only into that circle, very hard; moving the circle means unanchoring first.

adds_weaknesses.why: Anchored, it fires only into the one circle it picked; enemies who step out of it are safe until it anchors again.

variants.name: Become a structure
variants.summary: It unfolds into a small building that does a job for the team (a refinery, a healing post) and gives up its weapons until it packs up.
variants.seen_in: Yuri's Revenge Slave Miner (refinery), Red Alert 3 Engineer (first-aid tent)

adds_strengths.why: Deployed, it becomes a tough little building that does a job for the team, such as healing or income.

adds_weaknesses.why: As a building it can't move or fight back, and infiltrators and demolition charges treat it like any structure.

variants.name: Carried while planted
variants.summary: A teammate's transport can lift it while it is planted and set it down ready to fire after a short delay.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft II, Legacy of the Void's beta until patch 3.8 (medivacs carrying sieged tanks), and co-op dropships

adds_strengths.why: Planted, it gains more reach, firepower or armour than a mobile unit of its price, and holds the spot it chose.

adds_weaknesses.why: It can't move while planted, and setting up and packing up take time, so divers and artillery catch it.

counters.why: Slow ground units have to walk into its prepared field of fire and can't get out of it quickly.
Planted, it out-reaches units with shorter guns and hits them before they can reply, as long as they come at it head-on.

countered_by.why: Most planted modes only hit the ground, and fliers ignore the spot it holds.
Fast flankers get behind its arc or inside its blind zone before it can pack up.
Artillery and bombardment hit it easily, because a planted unit can't dodge.

open_questions: On a card the deploy-anchor mobility trait already uses a key and stands for this pattern. Should the pattern also be listed as an ability (which counts the key twice), or appear only through the trait?

What forces a unit out of its planted mode: only hard disables (Overwatch's sentry Bastion was immune to knockback and left the mode when hacked, slept, pinned, hooked or knocked down), any stun as well, or nothing? (Recommended: pulls, knockdowns and stuns.)
May a player bail out of a planted vehicle and leave it as a crewable emplacement for a teammate?
Does a landed flier count as a ground target for every weapon, as in Red Alert 2, and how is that shown from above?
Should planted weapons that reach past the unit's own sight fire only at targets a teammate has spotted, or at anything on the team's shared view?

shooter_fit.reason: A clear, readable trade of mobility for power that shooters already use (PlanetSide 2's lockdown, Overwatch's Bastion) and that creates escort and dive play; a fully static player can stall a match, so set-up times, arcs and forced-out effects need tuning.
